doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Criticism of jazz education and what students don't learn
summary: He argues jazz courses neglect early jazz and standards, leaving young players ignorant of basics like Sweet Georgia Brown.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: The state of jazz in Australia: what’s the most contemporary thing that’s going on? Does it pretty much follow what goes on in the States?

I think so. The jazz education program there has a large bearing on the types of young people that come out. They go from high school to say the music programs in the colleges, and then out into the jazz workforce, if you like. And I think the way they teach jazz here is pretty much similar in the college here. It’s pretty much similar to the way they do it over there. And I don’t really think it’s a good thing because the way they teach is — I don’t really know what to say about that — but I’ve met a lot of young guys that have come up through jazz education courses and learned, and been in there for two or three years. And they don’t know the basics. They don’t know “Sweet Georgia Brown.” They get embarrassed. They come and sit in with a swing band and you call “Sweet Georgia Brown” and they don’t know it. I’m just touching on like sort of sore points here.
They’re not learning tunes, they’re learning chords.

They learn modes, they learn the chords, 2-5-1s, they learn how to improvise — I think the teachers — it’s not the students’ fault, it’s the teachers’ fault, and the people that design the curriculum, the curricula. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-

The syllabi. There you go. And the teachers they get know what they know and they pay a bit of lip service to the old masters. They go back maybe as far as Charlie Parker and they might touch on the seminal influences before, and Louis Armstrong, Bix Beiderbecke, Lester Young and maybe Coleman Hawkins and probably speak about ragtime or something. They mention the Original Dixieland Jazz Band as being the first to record. But from what I gather from friends of mine who have gone through these courses, they really don’t dwell on it enough. So the kids really don’t have any idea. And they really get into the meat and potatoes of jazz, after Parker, like post-bebop they really start studying in the post-bebop period, because that’s where the teachers come from. That’s what they know. And these are the sort of players that you see come up. Until recently most of the young players in Sydney have been out of this kind of education system, this mold, and it’s been the rare one that’s been able to sidestep it. But there’s a few guys that don’t want to do that or can’t do it. And they end up being professionals in our sort of thing. They can play traditional jazz. You know, if they play the trombone they know all about Kid Ory and they learn the proper songs and they don’t try and play bebop over the wrong sorts of music. So it’s a bit of a sore point with me there. Though I think the educational system is — getting back to the original question — probably similar to here.
